messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina is a 35-year-old married physical therapist who came to treatment months after leaving a violent boyfriend she had dated before her marriage, an experience she still speaks about in fragments. In the relationship, the abuse often came in ordinary domestic moments that turned suddenly coercive. He would grab her wrist or upper arm hard enough to stop her from walking away, pin her in place when she tried to end an argument, and force her to stay in the room while he berated her. What stayed with her most vividly was the feeling of heat on her skin during those episodes—the warmth of his hand clamped around her, the trapped, flushed sensation in her body when she could not move, and the unbearable certainty that her own wishes no longer mattered. Even now, when she tries to tell the story straight through, she loses the thread, skips over crucial parts, and then goes quiet because the emotion rises so fast she feels she cannot keep going.

In the years since, those memories have not settled into the past. A warm hand placed on her forearm during a routine interaction, a patient gripping her unexpectedly during therapy, even the specific sensation of heat against her skin can make the scene come back as if it is happening again. At work this is particularly difficult, because physical contact is built into the day. When a patient resists an exercise or clutches at her as she guides a movement, the bodily sense of being overruled returns immediately. In those moments she is not simply remembering; she feels seized by the old panic and humiliation, and afterward she often becomes preoccupied with preventing anything similar from happening again. She scans new patients and family members in the clinic for signs of volatility, watches closely for people who seem controlling, and mentally rehearses how she could avoid being cornered. She also finds herself dwelling on the person she was before the abuse, comparing that version of herself to who she believes she is now.

What frightens Mina almost as much as the memories is what they seem to say about her. When the episodes come back with such force and she cannot narrate them clearly, she takes that as evidence that something is wrong with her at a deeper level. She has come to believe the abuse happened because of the way she acted—that she should have spoken differently, left sooner, resisted better. The emotional flooding of recall leaves her feeling exposed and ashamed, as though the event revealed a defective part of her that other people might somehow see. She does not describe the abuse only as something terrible that happened to her; she describes it as something humiliating that marked her permanently.

That belief has shaped the way she moves through the world. Because she feels there is something flawed in her judgment and character, she spends long stretches mentally revisiting the relationship, trying to identify the exact moment she could have prevented it. She goes over arguments, gestures, and decisions, convinced that if she could just locate the mistake she made, she might protect herself from ever being trapped again. She also watches people intensely. In the clinic, if a patient’s spouse answers for them too quickly or a man stands too close in the treatment room, Mina’s attention narrows at once. Her vigilance is not abstract; it is driven by the conviction that she missed warning signs before and must not miss them again.

At the same time, those beliefs make the world feel easier to trigger. Because being physically overruled has become tied in her mind to personal weakness and humiliation, even small experiences of lost autonomy can sting with disproportionate force. A supervisor changing her schedule without much discussion, a patient refusing to follow instructions and grabbing her arm to redirect her, or even affectionate touch from her husband when she is not expecting it can ignite the old sense that her boundaries do not count. Warmth on her skin or an uninvited hand is no longer just sensation; it lands on a meaning she already carries about herself. In turn, the more she scans for dangerous or controlling people and the more she rehearses how things should have been prevented, the more quickly she notices touch, heat, and moments of being directed by others. Her world has become organized around anticipating those sensations before they arrive.

At home, she has become careful in ways her husband experiences as distance. She pulls away from casual touch unless she has initiated it, becomes tense if he urges her to do something when she is undecided, and later retreats into long, self-critical brooding about how different she used to be. What finally brought her to seek help was a recent incident at work when a patient, frustrated and off balance, grabbed both of her wrists during a transfer. Mina froze, felt the memory surge into the present, and had to leave the room in tears, unable afterward to explain coherently to her supervisor what had happened. She comes to treatment afraid that she has been fundamentally damaged and will always live at the mercy of touch, heat, and coercion, but also hoping that the past might someday feel like something over rather than something waiting to happen again.
